segments.text: Look up on a clear day. The sky is blue. But sunlight itself? White. So where does the blue actually come from?
The answer is written into the air itself — tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, each one far smaller than a wave of light.
When sunlight hits those molecules, they scatter short blue wavelengths in every direction — several times more strongly than they scatter red.
That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead. And that is why the whole sky glows blue.
Violet gets scattered even more. But there is less of it in sunlight to begin with, and your eyes are less sensitive to it.
At sunset, that sunlight crosses much more air. The blue gets scattered away along the way, and the reds and oranges remain.
Dust and pollution, on the other hand, scatter all colors equally. That is why a hazy sky looks pale and white.
So the blue sky is not a thing. It is sunlight, rearranged by the air. Thanks for watching.
